Outstanding returns rise from 0 in January to 48 in September 2026, because recent months' returns are still arriving. Any month-on-month trend ending at the latest month will understate it. The published figures are provisional by design, not wrong.

The waste balance is tonnage credited during the reporting month, which the regulator describes as issued PRNs plus tonnage eligible for issuance. It is a monthly flow, not a stock, so issuance in a month can exceed that month's credit by drawing on accumulated balance: this happens in 28 of 117 material-month-stream rows. Cumulative credit exceeds cumulative issuance for all seven materials, so there is no inconsistency to correct.

Over January to September 2026 cumulative tonnage recycled EXCEEDS cumulative tonnage received for two materials: glass other by 25,937 tonnes (191,275 recycled against 165,338 received, 15.7 per cent more) and paper and board by 66,015 tonnes (901,168 against 835,154, 7.9 per cent more). Material cannot be recycled before it is received, so the excess is stock held at the start of 2026 and processed during it. This is a measured floor on opening stock for those two materials, not the whole of it, because any stock still unprocessed at the extraction date is not captured. Within single months the same pattern appears in 31 of 63 material-months and is ordinary drawdown; the cumulative figure is the one that carries information.

Average price per tonne spans two orders of magnitude across materials in 2026: paper and board £1.50 to £8.94, plastic £234.09 to £876.30. The cost of discharging an obligation therefore depends overwhelmingly on which material it is in.
